This collectively points to Germany over neighboring countries like Austria or the Netherlands (different plate codes and sign details).

Ulm across the river uses “UL”, so seeing NU suggests the Bavarian side rather than Ulm (Baden‑Württemberg). The mid-rise postwar block architecture and tree-lined narrow streets are consistent with central Neu-Ulm neighborhoods. No tram tracks (common in Ulm center) helps lean to a calmer Neu-Ulm side street. 
Street level: The scene shows a one-way system ahead with a no-entry sign on the left branch and a yielding side street, plus a distinctive overhead streetlamp suspended by a cable across the carriageway. There are inset parallel parking bays with a low cobbled divider and planted shrub bed on the right, and multiple blue parking-zone signs clustered before the intersection. This specific combination—cable-suspended lamp, planted bay edge, and clustered German parking/one-way signage—helps distinguish this exact street segment within Neu-Ulm’s inner residential/commercial grid, rather than a main arterial or tram corridor.
